subject: Database Management Systems & SQL
exam_relevance: 8-10 questions expected in BPSC TRE CS exam

questions.question: In the three-schema (ANSI-SPARC) architecture of a DBMS, the three levels are:

options.B: Client, Application Server, and Database Server
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: ANSI-SPARC 3-schema DBMS architecture consists of External (view), Conceptual (logical), and Internal (physical) levels.

questions.question: Which level of the three-schema DBMS architecture describes how data is actually stored on physical storage devices?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The internal (physical) schema describes the physical storage structures, file organization, and access paths of the database.

questions.question: Logical data independence is the capacity to change the _____ without changing external schemas or application programs.

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Logical data independence means modifying the conceptual schema (e.g., adding tables/columns) without rewriting user views or apps.

questions.question: Physical data independence allows changing the _____ without affecting the conceptual schema.

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Physical data independence protects the conceptual schema from changes in physical storage or indexing (internal schema).

questions.question: In a three-tier web DBMS architecture, the middle tier between the client and the database server is the:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Three-tier web architecture consists of Client (presentation), Application Server (business logic), and Database Server (data).

questions.question: Which level of DBMS architecture provides customized views of the database to different end users?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The external (view) level defines user-specific views, hiding irrelevant details and enforcing security.

questions.question: Metadata (data about data), such as table definitions and constraints, is stored by a DBMS in the:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The data dictionary (system catalog) stores metadata describing schemas, tables, attributes, constraints, and permissions.

questions.question: Which of the following is an advantage of a DBMS over a traditional file-processing system?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: DBMS reduces redundancy, enforces integrity/security, and supports concurrency control and recovery—all three options are true.

questions.question: In the relational data model, a row of a table is formally called a:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: In relational terminology: table = relation, row = tuple, column = attribute.

questions.question: The set of permitted data values for each column in a relational database table is called a:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: A domain is the set of atomic, valid values allowed for an attribute (column). (BPSC TRE 2.0 actual question)

questions.question: The number of attributes (columns) in a relation is called its:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Degree (arity) = number of columns/attributes in a relation. Cardinality = number of rows/tuples.

questions.question: The number of tuples (rows) currently present in a relation is called its:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The number of tuples (rows) in a relation is called Cardinality (Degree = columns, Domain = allowed values).

questions.question: If relation R has 5 columns and 10 rows, and relation S has 3 columns and 4 rows, what are the degree and cardinality of R × S (Cartesian product)?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Cartesian product adds degrees (5+3=8) and multiplies cardinalities (10×4=40).

questions.question: Which data model organizes data in a tree-like parent-child structure where a child has at most one parent?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The hierarchical model represents 1:N relationships as a tree; each child node has only one parent (network allows many).

questions.question: Who proposed the Relational Data Model in 1970?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: E. F. Codd proposed the Relational Data Model in 1970 (Chen proposed ER model; Bachman proposed Network model).

questions.question: In relational databases, a NULL value in an attribute represents:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: NULL is not 0 or blank space; it denotes a missing, unknown, or inapplicable attribute value.

questions.question: A minimal super key (a super key with no redundant attributes) is called a:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: A candidate key is a minimal super key: it uniquely identifies tuples and no proper subset of it is a super key.

questions.question: Which constraint requires that values in an attribute of a referencing relation must appear in the referenced relation (or be NULL)?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Referential integrity ensures foreign key values match an existing primary/unique key in the referenced table. (BPSC TRE 1.0)

questions.question: Entity integrity constraint states that no attribute of a _____ can contain a NULL value.

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Entity integrity mandates that primary key attributes must be unique and NOT NULL so every tuple is uniquely identifiable.

questions.question: Candidate keys that are NOT chosen as the primary key of a relation are called:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Candidate keys not chosen as the primary key are called Alternate keys (or secondary keys).

questions.question: For relation Student(RollNo, Email, AadharNo, Name), where RollNo, Email, and AadharNo are each unique, how many candidate keys exist if RollNo is chosen as primary key?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: There are 3 candidate keys (RollNo, Email, AadharNo), 1 primary key (RollNo), and 2 alternate keys (Email, AadharNo). All A, B, C are true.

questions.question: Which statement is TRUE about a Primary Key and a Foreign Key?

options.A: A table can have at most one Primary Key
options.B: A table can have multiple Foreign Keys
options.C: A Foreign Key can accept duplicate and NULL values (unless restricted)
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: A relation has one primary key, may have multiple foreign keys, and foreign keys can contain duplicates or NULLs.

questions.question: Every _____ is a super key, though the converse is not always true.

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Every candidate key is a minimal super key, though not every super key is minimal (hence not always a candidate key).

questions.question: In relation R(A, B, C, D) with A as the sole candidate key, how many super keys does R have?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Any subset containing A is a super key. With 3 remaining attributes {B,C,D}, there are 2^3 = 8 super keys.

questions.question: A primary key that consists of two or more attributes combined together is called a:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: A composite key uses two or more attributes together (e.g., (StudentID, CourseID)) to uniquely identify a tuple.

questions.question: An attribute that is part of at least one candidate key is known as a:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Prime attributes belong to at least one candidate key; attributes not in any candidate key are non-prime.

questions.question: If a referenced tuple in a parent table is deleted, which foreign key action automatically deletes matching rows in the child table?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: ON DELETE CASCADE propagates deletion from parent to child rows; SET NULL sets FK to NULL; RESTRICT blocks deletion.

questions.question: A super key of a relation R is a set of attributes that:

options.A: Cannot contain more than two attributes
options.B: Uniquely identifies each tuple in R
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: A super key uniquely identifies tuples in a relation and may contain extra redundant attributes (minimality makes it a candidate key).

questions.question: A relation is in First Normal Form (1NF) if and only if:

options.A: All attribute domains contain only atomic (indivisible) values
options.B: There are no repeating groups or multivalued attributes
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: 1NF requires atomic values in every cell and no repeating groups/multivalued attributes. Both A and B define 1NF.

questions.question: Second Normal Form (2NF) removes which type of functional dependency?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: 2NF requires 1NF and no partial dependency (no non-prime attribute depends on a proper subset of a candidate key).

questions.question: Third Normal Form (3NF) eliminates which type of dependency among non-prime attributes?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: 3NF requires 2NF and no transitive dependency (non-prime attribute depending on another non-prime attribute).

questions.question: A relation is in Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) if for every non-trivial functional dependency X → Y:

options.B: X is a proper subset of a candidate key
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: BCNF requires the determinant X (left side) to be a super key for every non-trivial FD X -> Y.

questions.question: If a relation in 1NF has a single-attribute candidate key (no composite candidate keys), then it is automatically in:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Partial dependency requires a proper subset of a composite key; with single-attribute keys, 1NF is automatically in 2NF.

questions.question: Which anomalies can occur in an unnormalized database table?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Redundancy in unnormalized tables causes insertion, deletion, and update anomalies—normalization reduces all three.

questions.question: Which normal form is strictly stronger than 3NF?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Hierarchy: 1NF ⊃ 2NF ⊃ 3NF ⊃ BCNF. Every BCNF relation is in 3NF, but not every 3NF relation is in BCNF.

questions.question: In relation R(A, B, C) with candidate key (A, B), the functional dependency B → C is an example of:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Non-prime C depends on B, a proper subset of candidate key (A,B), which is a partial dependency violating 2NF.

questions.question: In relation R(EmpID, DeptID, DeptName) with candidate key EmpID and FDs EmpID → DeptID, DeptID → DeptName, R is in:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: EmpID is a single key (so 2NF holds), but EmpID → DeptID → DeptName is a transitive dependency, so R is not in 3NF.

questions.question: Fourth Normal Form (4NF) is concerned with eliminating:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: 4NF eliminates non-trivial multivalued dependencies (MVDs); partial=2NF, transitive=3NF, join=5NF.

questions.question: Fifth Normal Form (5NF), also called Project-Join Normal Form (PJNF), deals with:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: 5NF (PJNF) eliminates redundancy caused by join dependencies so tables decompose losslessly.

questions.question: Which two properties are desirable when decomposing a relation during normalization?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Good schema decomposition ensures lossless-join (no spurious tuples) and dependency preservation (A and B).

questions.question: Which normal form always guarantees both lossless-join and dependency-preserving decomposition for any set of functional dependencies?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Every relation can be decomposed into 3NF with both lossless-join and dependency preservation; BCNF may sacrifice dependency preservation.

questions.question: In functional dependency X → Y, X is called the _____ and Y is called the dependent.

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: In X → Y (X functionally determines Y), the left-hand side X is the determinant.

questions.question: Which of Armstrong's axioms states that if X → Y and Y → Z, then X → Z?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Armstrong's three inference axioms are Reflexivity (Y⊆X ⇒ X→Y), Augmentation (X→Y ⇒ XZ→YZ), and Transitivity (X→Y, Y→Z ⇒ X→Z).

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a constraint in SQL?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: UNION is a set operator combining SELECT results, not a table constraint. PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE are constraints. (BPSC TRE 1.0)

questions.question: Which SQL commands belong to Data Definition Language (DDL)?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, and TRUNCATE are all DDL commands (define/modify structure). INSERT and UPDATE are DML.

questions.question: What is the key difference between TRUNCATE TABLE and DELETE FROM table?

options.A: TRUNCATE is a DDL command that removes all rows without a WHERE clause
options.B: DELETE is a DML command that can use a WHERE clause to remove specific rows
options.C: DROP removes both table data and structure, whereas TRUNCATE keeps the structure
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: All three statements A, B, and C accurately distinguish TRUNCATE, DELETE, and DROP in standard SQL.

questions.question: Which SQL command is used to add a new column to an existing table?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: ALTER TABLE table_name ADD col datatype; is used in SQL to add a new column to an existing table.

questions.question: Which SQL constraint ensures that a column cannot store a NULL value?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: NOT NULL rejects NULL values in the column. UNIQUE allows NULL (in standard SQL) while enforcing uniqueness.

questions.question: Which SQL constraint validates that values inserted into a column satisfy a specified condition (e.g., age >= 18)?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The CHECK constraint enforces domain conditions such as CHECK (age >= 18) on inserted or updated rows.

questions.question: Which SQL command permanently deletes a table's data as well as its schema/definition from the database?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: DROP TABLE removes both the data and the table definition completely; TRUNCATE and DELETE keep the table structure.

questions.question: Which SQL constraint assigns a predefined value to a column when no value is supplied during INSERT?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The DEFAULT constraint assigns a predefined value when no value is supplied during INSERT.

questions.question: Which SQL command creates a virtual table based on the result-set of a SELECT query?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: A view is a virtual table defined by a stored SQL query using CREATE VIEW view_name AS SELECT ...

questions.question: How many UNIQUE constraints can a single SQL table have?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: A table can have only one PRIMARY KEY, but it can have multiple UNIQUE constraints.

questions.question: Which SQL commands are classified as Data Manipulation Language (DML)?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE (and SELECT in many textbooks) are DML commands used to manipulate table rows.

questions.question: Which SQL keyword is used to sort the result-set of a SELECT query?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: ORDER BY sorts output rows (ASC by default, or DESC). GROUP BY groups rows for aggregation.

questions.question: Which SQL clause is used to filter groups created by GROUP BY based on aggregate conditions?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping; HAVING filters grouped rows after GROUP BY and supports aggregate functions.

questions.question: In SQL, what is the default sort order of the ORDER BY clause when neither ASC nor DESC is specified?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: ORDER BY sorts in ascending order (ASC) by default; DESC must be written explicitly for descending order.

questions.question: What happens if an UPDATE statement is executed without a WHERE clause?

options.A: All rows in the table are updated
options.C: Only the first row is updated
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Omitting WHERE in UPDATE (or DELETE) applies the operation to every single row in the table.

questions.question: Which SQL operator checks whether a value falls within a specified inclusive range?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: BETWEEN low AND high matches values >= low and <= high (inclusive of both boundary values).

questions.question: To check if a column value is NULL in a SQL WHERE clause, which syntax is correct?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Comparing with = NULL always evaluates to UNKNOWN; SQL requires IS NULL or IS NOT NULL.

questions.question: What is the logical execution order of clauses in a SQL SELECT query?

options.A: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY
options.B: SELECT → FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → ORDER BY
options.C: FROM → GROUP BY → WHERE → SELECT → HAVING → ORDER BY
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: SQL evaluates FROM first, filters rows via WHERE, forms groups (GROUP BY), filters groups (HAVING), projects (SELECT), then sorts (ORDER BY).

questions.question: Which SQL statement is used to insert new rows into an existing table?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: INSERT INTO table_name ... VALUES ... is the standard SQL statement to insert new rows.

questions.question: Which SQL operator tests whether a value matches any value in a list or subquery?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: IN compares a value against a list or single-column subquery (e.g., WHERE dept IN ('CS', 'IT')).

questions.question: Which SQL command modifies existing data values inside rows of a table?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: UPDATE table_name SET col = val WHERE ... modifies row data (DML), whereas ALTER modifies table schema (DDL).

questions.question: In SQL, GRANT and REVOKE belong to which sublanguage?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: GRANT and REVOKE are DCL (Data Control Language) commands used to manage user privileges and access rights.

questions.question: What does SELECT * FROM Employee; return?

options.A: Only the primary key column of Employee
options.B: Only the column names without data
options.C: All columns and all rows of the Employee table
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The wildcard * in SELECT * projects every attribute of the table, and without WHERE it returns all rows.

questions.question: Which SQL query finds the second highest salary from an Employee(Salary) table?

options.A: SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Employee WHERE Salary < (SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Employee);
options.B: SELECT MIN(Salary) FROM Employee WHERE Salary > (SELECT MIN(Salary) FROM Employee);
options.C: SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Employee WHERE Salary = (SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Employee);
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Taking MAX(Salary) strictly less than the overall MAX(Salary) yields the second highest distinct salary.

questions.question: Which SQL clause is used to remove duplicate rows from the result of a SELECT query?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: SELECT DISTINCT column_name removes duplicate values from the query output.

questions.question: What will the SQL query SELECT ROUND(65.726, -1) FROM DUAL; output?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Negative second argument -1 rounds to the nearest 10 (tens place): 65.726 rounds up to 70. (BPSC TRE 1.0 actual question)

questions.question: Which SQL keyword is used to display data matching a specified character pattern?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: LIKE performs pattern matching using % (zero or more chars) and _ (single char). (BPSC TRE 2.0 actual question)

questions.question: In SQL LIKE pattern matching, which wildcard characters are standard?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Standard SQL LIKE uses % for zero or more characters and _ for a single character. Both A and B are correct.

questions.question: How do COUNT(*) and COUNT(column_name) differ in SQL?

options.A: Both always return the exact same number even when NULLs exist
options.B: COUNT(*) counts all rows including NULLs, while COUNT(column_name) ignores NULL values
options.C: COUNT(*) ignores NULL rows, while COUNT(column_name) counts NULLs
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts every row in the table/group; COUNT(col) counts only rows where col is NOT NULL.

questions.question: Which of the following are SQL aggregate functions?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX, and MIN are the five standard SQL aggregate functions (both A and B). ROUND/LENGTH are scalar functions.

questions.question: If a column Marks has values {10, 20, NULL, 30}, what does AVG(Marks) return in SQL?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Aggregate functions (except COUNT(*)) ignore NULLs: (10 + 20 + 30) / 3 = 60 / 3 = 20.

questions.question: Why is SELECT Name FROM Emp WHERE AVG(Salary) > 50000; invalid in SQL?

options.A: WHERE cannot be used with SELECT statements
options.B: AVG() only works on character columns
options.C: Aggregate functions cannot be used directly in a WHERE clause
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping; aggregate conditions must be placed in a HAVING clause.

questions.question: Which SQL pattern in LIKE matches any string of at least 3 characters?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Three underscores (___) require 3 characters, and % allows 0 or more additional characters, matching length >= 3.

questions.question: What does SELECT ROUND(123.456, 2); return?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: ROUND(123.456, 2) rounds to 2 decimal places; since the 3rd digit is 6 (>=5), it rounds up to 123.46.

questions.question: Which SQL function returns the number of characters in a string?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: LENGTH() / CHAR_LENGTH() / LEN() returns string character count; COUNT, SUM, MAX are aggregate functions.

questions.question: Which SQL JOIN returns only the rows that have matching values in both tables?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: INNER JOIN (the default JOIN) returns only tuples where the join condition matches in both tables.

questions.question: A LEFT OUTER JOIN between table A and table B returns:

options.A: Only rows matching in both A and B
options.B: All rows from A, and matching rows from B (with NULLs for B when there is no match)
options.C: All rows from B, and matching rows from A
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: LEFT OUTER JOIN preserves all rows from the left table (A) and fills unmatched right-table (B) columns with NULL.

questions.question: Which join produces the Cartesian product of two tables when no join condition is specified?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: CROSS JOIN pairs every row of the first table with every row of the second table (Cartesian product).

questions.question: Joining a table with itself (for example, Employee joined with Employee to find each employee's manager) is called a:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Joining a table with itself using table aliases is called a SELF JOIN.

questions.question: How does NATURAL JOIN work between two tables?

options.C: Requires an explicit ON join condition
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: NATURAL JOIN implicitly performs an equijoin on common attribute names and retains only one copy of each common column.

questions.question: What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL in SQL?

options.A: UNION requires tables to have different numbers of columns
options.B: UNION eliminates duplicate rows, whereas UNION ALL retains all duplicate rows
options.C: UNION ALL eliminates duplicates, whereas UNION keeps them
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: UNION performs duplicate elimination (set union); UNION ALL keeps all rows from both queries and is faster.

questions.question: For UNION of two SELECT queries to be valid, what must be true (union compatibility)?

options.A: Both queries must select the same number of columns
options.B: Corresponding columns must have compatible data types
options.C: Both tables must have the same number of rows
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Union compatibility requires the same number of columns (A) and compatible data types in corresponding positions (B).

questions.question: Which join returns all rows from both the left and right tables, placing NULLs where matches do not exist on either side?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: FULL OUTER JOIN combines LEFT and RIGHT outer joins, keeping unmatched rows from both tables with NULL padding.

questions.question: If table A has 3 rows and table B has 4 rows with no matching keys, how many rows are returned by A LEFT OUTER JOIN B?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: LEFT OUTER JOIN preserves all 3 rows from left table A, pairing them with NULLs for table B columns.

questions.question: Which SQL set operator returns only rows that appear in BOTH SELECT query results?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: INTERSECT returns common rows present in both queries; EXCEPT/MINUS returns rows in the first query not in the second.

questions.question: In DBMS transactions, what does the acronym ACID stand for?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: ACID stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability—the four core properties of database transactions.

questions.question: Which ACID property guarantees that a transaction executes completely (all operations) or not at all (rolled back)?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Atomicity ('all-or-nothing') guarantees a transaction executes completely or rolls back entirely.

questions.question: Which ACID property ensures that once a transaction commits, its changes survive system crashes or power failures?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Durability guarantees committed updates are permanently stored in non-volatile memory (via logs/disk) even after crashes.

questions.question: Which ACID property ensures that concurrent execution of transactions yields the same result as serial execution without interference?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Isolation prevents concurrent transactions from observing each other's uncommitted intermediate states.

questions.question: Which SQL commands belong to Transaction Control Language (TCL)?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: COMMIT, ROLLBACK, and SAVEPOINT are TCL commands (both A and B). CREATE and DROP are DDL.

questions.question: Which SQL command undoes all uncommitted changes in the current transaction (or back to a SAVEPOINT)?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: ROLLBACK aborts/undoes uncommitted changes; COMMIT makes them permanent.

questions.question: Which DBMS components are primarily responsible for ensuring Atomicity and Durability?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The recovery manager (using undo/redo logs) enforces Atomicity and Durability; concurrency control enforces Isolation.

questions.question: A schedule of concurrent transactions is called conflict-serializable if:

options.A: It is conflict-equivalent to some serial schedule
options.B: Its precedence (serialization) graph has no cycles
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: A schedule is conflict-serializable iff it is conflict-equivalent to a serial schedule, tested by an acyclic precedence graph (A & B).

questions.question: In an Entity-Relationship (ER) diagram, what shapes represent an Entity Set, a Relationship Set, and an Attribute respectively?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Standard Chen ER notation uses Rectangle for Entity Set, Diamond for Relationship Set, and Ellipse/Oval for Attribute.

questions.question: A weak entity set in an ER model is represented by a _____ and has a _____ rather than its own primary key.

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: A weak entity set depends on an owner/identifying entity, is drawn as a double rectangle, and uses a partial key (dashed underline).

questions.question: In an ER diagram, an attribute that can be calculated from another attribute (e.g., Age from Date of Birth) is called a _____ attribute and is drawn as a _____.

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Derived attributes (e.g., Age from DOB) use a dashed ellipse; multivalued attributes (e.g., PhoneNumbers) use a double ellipse.

questions.question: When converting a Many-to-Many (M:N) binary relationship between two strong entity sets into relational tables, how many tables are required?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: An M:N relationship requires a separate third relation containing the primary keys of both participating entity sets.
